newsitem.title: GERMANY: Embattled Waigel says EMU a historic project.
newsitem.headline: Embattled Waigel says EMU a historic project.

text.p: Finance Minister Theo Waigel, shaken by attacks on steps he is taking to get Germany fit for European monetary union (EMU), sought on Monday to refocus on the project's historic dimension.

Shrugging off rows over budget deficits and accusations of creative accounting, Waigel said Europe had a rare chance to cast off decades of turmoil and war and build a secure future for the 21st century.
"We have the first chance to establish a Europe of freedom and peace where we can tell the next generation that what our mothers and fathers suffered can't happen again," he said in a speech.

Waigel, struggling to contain state borrowing to meet the tight targets set by the Maastricht treaty, even cited former U.S. Secretary of State Henry Kissinger, saying there were "only a few moments in each century when there is a chance to shape the destiny of the next century".

Waigel, himself an architect of the Maastricht treaty, said that Germans overwhelmingly supported the European ideal. Only when it came to giving up their beloved deutschemark, did the population give a resounding "no".

But an independent European central bank, a stability pact to enforce sound state finances and the tough Maastricht treaty criteria will ensure the euro is stable, he told an audience of fellow Christian Democrat deputies to the European parliament.

Waigel is struggling to cut Germany's budget deficit to the goal of three percent of gross domestic product stipulated by Maastricht, and has clashed with junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP) over taxes.
Although the FDP at a weekend party conference adopted a motion rejecting tax rises, Waigel again refused to have his hands tied.
"A Finance Minister who rules this and that out now would not be in a position to take effective action. No responsible Finance Minister can rule that out," he told reporters.

He also defended as prudent his plan to revalue the Bundesbank's gold and foreign exchange reserves closer to market levels -- as would be required in any case when the planned European central bank is created. Bonn says the scheme would help cut both the deficit and the national debt.
"The reorganisation of the accounts of the Bundesbank will be undertaken with the required caution," he said. "The financial solidity of the Bundesbank will be maintained.
Waigel said Bonn would continue to insist on a tight interpretation of the Maastricht treaty to ensure the planned euro currency is stable.
Any debate on allowing the three percent deficit goal to be interpreted loosely would be the start of a slippery slope.
"For the government, a narrow and strict applicaton of the treaty rules when examining convergence is vital. Markets and citizens expect that," he said.
Waigel also said it would be wrong to pre-empt the decision to be made by European leaders in a year's time on which countries would join EMU at the planned 1999 start.
"Convergence dictates the timetable -- for every single country," Waigel said. Until then, "speculation over the group of members would be pointless".

He also said no countries should get special treatment. "A chain is only as strong as its weakest link. Therefore, only equally strong stability-based (countries) can join the start of currency union," he said.
Waigel added it would be possible for countries to join later after pressing on with efforts to converge with the EMU "ins" as members of a revised European exchange rate mechanism.
"Nobody will suffer discrimination or be left behind," he said. "The euro-countries will offer all the others an anchor of stability."
